title: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says
description: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migratio
body: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered."This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.

schema.headline: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says

title: Robert Pattinson on new film Primetime and how hunting predators became hit TV
description: Robert Pattinson is having quite the year.The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbu
body: Robert Pattinson is having quite the year.The British actor has already starred opposite Zendaya in The Drama, and played a key role in summer blockbuster The Odyssey.But his new film, Primetime, takes him in a completely new direction - as he portrays the real-life host of American TV show, To Catch a Predator.The show, which aired from 2004 to 2007, involved hunting alleged child abusers.For Pattinson, who became a father almost three years ago, the film's plot is particularly concerning."It's both the most terrifying thing that can happen to you, whether you're a parent, or even if you're not," he told BBC News at the film's screening at London Film Festival."It's the most unimaginable sin possible," he added.Robert Pattinson: Being a dad makes life 'more fun'The new A24 crime thriller depicts the show's host, NBC journalist Chris Hansen, carrying out sting operations on would-be predators.The show was a ratings hit.But it also led to questions over where to draw the line between investigative journalism, police activity and reality television.Speaking on Sunday night, Pattinson reflected on the show's complicated legacy."The show was this kind of microcosm of saying, 'oh, we can do something about [child abuse], and we can do something about it really, really, really quickly," he said."And in some ways, that's correct, but it also makes for incredibly powerful TV, and that's when it gets into slightly dicey territory."Pattinson, 40, became something of a pin-up after playing vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight series, alongside American actress Kristen Stewart.Before that, he stole young hearts as Hufflepuff hunk Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.He has since starred in major films including Christopher Nolan's Tenet, as well as a range of eccentric, indie films.This year, he has been on a roll, with Dune: Part Three still to come.He’s also got the next Batman film in the pipeline, although production on that has reportedly paused, external. When asked when they'll be back to work, Pattinson didn’t give much away ("We don't know yet, but yeah, working on it.")Primetime has also led to speculation that this could be the year that Pattinson gets his first ever Oscars nomination. Is that likely, I wonder?"I am eternally grateful that I got these jobs," he responds."But then [to have] been able to even do them, this is one of the best years of my life."

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson on new film Primetime and how hunting predators became hit TV

title: Man City: Prime Minister Andy Burnham to release details of his meetings with Man City owners
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City following criticism of his comment
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City following criticism of his comments in the wake of the club being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanding No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club."I've been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I'm happy to do and I'm going to," Burnham told the Rest is Politics podcast. "I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester. "None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."The prime minister initially told the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up following the guilty verdict before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process. Sanctions are yet to be announced and City have lodged an appeal against the verdict.City returned to action for the first time since the guilty verdict when they played at Liverpool on Sunday, winning 3-0.Burnham was mayor of Manchester from 2017 until earlier this year and his tenure took place during a sustained period of success for City.As mayor, he championed investment from the Gulf as a way of growing Manchester's economy, a strategy which was initially pursued by the city's leaders before Burnham became the inaugural elected mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority."I don't think I misspoke," said Burnham of his past comments on Man City's owners. "What I would say is my mind hadn't been on all of the issues. My mind had been on Labour Party conference and I was doing interviews in relation to it."And also, I didn't link those two things. You know, the questions linked those two things. What I would say is they're very separate."The football issues are different from the investment issues. People will try and conflate those two things, but they shouldn't, in my view. "The football issues, the findings of the independent commission are serious, as I said in the interview."The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League.An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.The commission's report said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".A separate independent appeal board will hear City's appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing.

schema.headline: Man City: Prime Minister Andy Burnham to release details of his meetings with Man City owners

title: Australia v South Africa: Pace attack and Steve Smith put tourists in charge
description: Australia veterans shine against South AfricaImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steve Smith now has 223 catches in Test cricket, three more than
body: Australia veterans shine against South AfricaImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steve Smith now has 223 catches in Test cricket, three more than Joe Root in second place for non-wicketkeepersByMatthew HenryBBC Sport JournalistFirst Test, Durban (day three of five)Australia 390 & 33-0: Maddinson 17*South Africa 284: Bedingham 49; Cummins 3-54Australia lead by 139 runsScorecardAustralia's modern Test side remain a fascinating one to unpick.Viewed by many in England as there for the taking in last winter's Ashes despite a 4-1 win, they are also labelled too old by many observers at home.The victims of recent shock defeats by West Indies and Bangladesh, they are still unbeaten in their past nine Test series.But while their struggling batting line-up was bailed out by Matt Renshaw across the first two days of the first Test in Durban, they took control over South Africa on day three in an all-too familiar way.Nine years after they first appeared together as Australia's bowling quartet, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon produced their latest relentless performance to dismiss South Africa for 284. There was even some magic from Steve Smith thrown in too.Cummins took three wickets, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon two apiece, in doing so brushing off any doubts about their effectiveness at the start of a run of Tests against the world Test champions, in-form New Zealand, India and England.How Australia's quartet turned the screw on South AfricaAt 82-1 in response to Australia's 390, South Africa appeared well in the Test on a relatively good surface.Australia's bowlers searched for early swing and Aiden Markram and David Bedingham countered with a second-wicket partnership which progressed at almost 4.5 runs per over.It was then, at the 20-over mark, captain Cummins reverted to Australia's tried and tested - Lyon one end, the quicks rotating at the other.Having bowled 34% of their deliveries full in the first 20 overs, Starc, Hazlewood and Cummins dragged back their lengths. There were only 19 deliveries pitched fuller than six metres between the 20th and 60th overs.With deliveries easy to hit scarce, Markram and Bedingham attempted forced back-foot drives and edged to slip for 37 and 49 respectively.Image source, CricVizImage caption, South Africa were 82-1 after 20 overs (left graphic) but were 214-8 after Australia dragged their lengths back between the 21st and 60th overs (right graphic)Wiaan Mulder was caught in two minds and bounced out by Cummins. Tristan Stubbs top-edged the Australia captain to fine leg.In Australia's first innings, Renshaw, who ground out a superb 190, faced 52 deliveries pitched as short and played a pull or hook shot to four of them. He scored runs with only one of those shots - when he had 176 runs to his name and had faced 368 balls.The contrast to Renshaw's application could not have been greater.Six overs after Stubbs was caught, Marco Jansen, who had struck six fours in quickly reaching 26, also tried to pull Hazlewood off a fuller length and was tamely caught at mid-off.The quality of the bowling and fact the Proteas are playing their first Test since November were other factors in South Africa's slide.Smith soars back to number oneAt the other end, off-spinner Lyon bowled 19 overs at less than three runs per over.The 39-year-old had a more worn pitch to utilise than South Africa's spinners and found significantly more turn and threat.He also had the sprawling Steve Smith to his advantage.Both of Smith's catches off Lyon, first to dismiss Temba Bavuma and then Kyle Verreynne, were feats of anticipation. He saw both right-handers shape to reverse sweep, gambled and clung on at close range. The first was good. The one-handed second was spectacular."He's an absolute freak," said Lyon. "He practices that in training."He is an incredible thinker of the game but the way he moves, premeditates, for those types of catches."There are not many people in the dressing room that would be able to pull off those two catches."In between, Smith's leaping catch at second slip after Cummins found Bedingham's edge took the 37-year-old back above Joe Root as the non-wicketkeeper with the most catches in Test history on 223.While he ended the day with three more catches than Root, he still has a catch percentage about 77%, which sits below the format average.He creates, and occasionally drops, chances such as these - chances others would not have created.Pace cartel appears as good as everThe result is Australia's fabled foursome now have 607 wickets in Tests in which they have played as a quartet.The next most successful bowling four-pronged attack is James Anderson, Stuart Broad, Ben Stokes and Moeen Ali, who took 415 wickets in their 31 Tests together for England."Each of these players will go down as a legend of Australian cricket," said former Australia bowler Jason Gillespie on ABC Radio."Starc got hit for a few early but I didn't mind that. "Hazlewood was very good, as he always is. Cummins was hostile. He looked fresh."Much has been made of Australia's ageing side and a perceived lack of succession planning.At 37, Starc is the oldest of the three quicks but his average pace of 141.21km/h in 2026 is higher than any of his past three years. He is also averaging his most swing in a calendar year since 2015.The concern for Australia comes when they are not fit, with Hazlewood having missed all five of last winter's Ashes Tests and Cummins four.Australia's issue right now is keeping each of their quartet on the field, because they appear as good as ever.At 33-0, Australia lead South Africa by 139 runs.Even with bad light halting play early again, they should have the time to press home an advantage across the Test's final two days.

schema.headline: Australia v South Africa: Pace attack and Steve Smith put tourists in charge

title: Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
description: The attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.Saudi Arabia
body: The attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this. In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease.Saturday's attack killed 12 people and hurt more than 300. On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said an "unknown projectile" had hit a passenger hall and a cruise missile had been intercepted nearby.The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering.As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait.The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel.Not since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat. The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen. It even shrugged off – with some annoyance – an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March.But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the country, particularly in the north and west.But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy.As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy.The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war.Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran.In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia.However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen.Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis. "We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said.But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month.When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters.This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement.Additional analysis from Abdelbassir Hassan, BBC Arabic

schema.headline: Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict

title: Legoland Windsor evacuated over burst water main
description: The Legoland Windsor attraction has closed abruptly due to a burst water main.Customers were told to leave rides and exit the resort at lunchtime on S
body: The Legoland Windsor attraction has closed abruptly due to a burst water main.Customers were told to leave rides and exit the resort at lunchtime on Sunday.Thames Water said it had to shut off the damaged main near St Leonards Reservoir to prevent flooding, which affected supplies to the theme park.It said some local residents had reportedly suffered flooded gardens and it apologised for the disruption.Merlin Entertainments, the operator behind Legoland, said it is continuing to work with local partners and thanked guests for their "patience and understanding".One Legoland visitor, who came with her children from Cornwall, said the sudden evacuation felt "surreal".The woman, who asked not to be named, said: "We were queuing for a ride and had got right to the front when, all of a sudden, everything stopped moving. "Then they came out and said, 'Right, come on, everybody off.' "Over the announcement system, they said there had been some sort of Thames Water disruption in the local area and they didn't have any water."We'd booked a night in the hotel and stayed there last night, so we're absolutely gutted because we've just had to drive home."It's a good five-hour drive to come up for a nice day, only to come back after half a day."Thames Water said supplies had been restored and repairs were under way. It said it would provide an update on Monday.A spokesperson for Merlin Entertainments said the resort was closed while Thames Water worked to restore normal service."We apologise for the inconvenience and thank our guests for their patience and understanding," the group said.The BBC understands the resort will reopen on Monday under normal operating hours.

schema.headline: Legoland Windsor evacuated over burst water main

title: Manchester City: A statement win but does it carry weight in a season of limbo?
description: Man City's statement win has feeling of irrelevance with season in limboImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Liverpool fans express their disgust
body: Man City's statement win has feeling of irrelevance with season in limboImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Liverpool fans express their disgust towards Manchester City during the Premier League game at AnfieldByChief football writer at AnfieldManchester City made what they will regard as a powerful statement in the most hostile territory against Liverpool at Anfield - but is it a statement that carries any weight during a Premier League season in limbo?City's attention turned to on-field matters in their first game since being found guilty of 114 charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18.The fates, and fixture list, decreed it would be at Liverpool, whose fans nurse the most burning sense of injustice after finishing second to City in 2013-14, 2018-19 and 2021-22.Their argument centres on the belief those titles could have been theirs had City not possessed the high finance of their Abu Dhabi-based owners, using it in the manner that led to them being investigated.With this as the backdrop, City strode into this fevered Anfield atmosphere, with Liverpool fans high on adrenaline and determined to make their contempt for their rivals obvious - then outclassed Andoni Iraola's side in a 3-0 win.On another day, in other circumstances, the manner of City's victory would have fed the narrative that this was a performance of champions, a winning marker laid down to their rivals as they hold a three-point lead at the top of the table.Not here. Not in the Premier League's dysfunctional state.Instead, once the predictable sound and fury had been diluted by City's composure and the swift realisation they were not unnerved by Anfield or the storm raging around the club, this was a surreal experience.After the feast of excitement delivered when Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp presided over the greatest domestic rivalry of recent years, this was an occasion - remarkable as it seems - that seemed robbed of a sense of jeopardy by the circumstances surrounding it.Yes, it was a statement display and City celebrated wildly at the final whistle, but will it count for anything given they await potential sanctions suggested including Premier League relegation or a record points deduction?Figure caption, What's going to happen to Manchester City?As Erling Haaland looked close to tears in front of Manchester City's fans, including his father Alf-Inge, and head coach Enzo Maresca pumped his fists in jubilation, Anfield's DJ slipped Fleetwood Mac's 'Little Lies' on to the loudspeakers in a final message of defiance.Maresca said: "We knew there was going to be noise but we need to make our own noise by winning games. We need to learn to deal with the noise but the message is to win games."For me it's quite easy. I try to focus on things I can control. There are things that are not in my hands so I don't stress about them."I cannot control things outside football, so why stress? I stress about gameplan, day-by-day training sessions, but the rest it's not in my hands."Haaland added: "For every single person part of Manchester City, every fan, this is a lovely moment that will stay with us for a long time. It was tough. It was hard, but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone."It's always tough to come here. If you look at the record it's tough. With the Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp era it was tough for both teams, always has been. It was important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about. The thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That's the only thing we can do."City have appealed against the verdict, but until the dust settles and final decisions are made, this Premier League season is in a holding pattern.When City come to Anfield and win, especially as convincingly as they did here, it should be a win without qualification or questions.This does not apply amid the current uncertainty.Every victory, every league table, will come with a metaphorical asterisk until clarity and finality comes. No-one knows when this will be.Figure caption, MOTD analysis - why Doku proved key in Man City's win at LiverpoolCity's players did their jobs to perfection, victory secured by second-half goals from Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki. It is all they can do.There can be no escape, however, from the cloud hanging over Manchester City because every win will carry the same rider - producing a state of inertia that is not good for the Premier League.In the end, a day that promised huge discomfort for City ended in a stroll.City navigated the hostile reception awaiting them at Anfield by arriving through the staff and contractors' entrance - while an inevitable febrile environment awaited them.Even the derided half-and-half scarves were doing a roaring trade, until it was noticed the sky blue half read: 'Shamchester City - The Cheats'.The announcement of City's line-up was drowned out by deafening jeers, while banners around Anfield carried a variety of messages.They including 'A Generation Of Supporters Cheated', 'And After All You Really Robbed Us All' and - in a nod to the Oasis song Stop Crying Your Heart Out, written by Noel Gallagher who was at Anfield, 'All Of Your Stars Are Fading Away'.This was all watched by an impassive City chief executive Ferran Soriano, but any notion their fans would turn on the owners was dispelled by a flag reading: 'In Khaldoon We Trust. We've Won It All', a gesture of support for the embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.City's fans also waved hundreds of inflatable bananas, an old habit when they spent time in the lower leagues in reduced circumstances. There remains the possibility they will get the chance to wave them down the tiers once more in the near future.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester City fans expressed support for chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at AnfieldThe first half did much to pour cold water on what started as a red-hot atmosphere, further diluted by City's second-half domination, although Liverpool's fans rammed home their disgust until the final whistle, chanting "cheat" every time their opponents passed in a lengthy period of possession.Former Liverpool and England defender Stephen Warnock told BBC Radio 5 Live: "This needs rectifying as quickly as possible, but this isn't an easy thing to come to a conclusion. It's never-ending. It's so difficult and it's going to take so long to sort out."He added: "The hard part is that this is a brilliant Manchester City team, but you have to caveat it and say they have done it illegally and they bought their way. You're caught in what you're thinking about this City team."I admire them because they're so good individually and so great, but the way it has been done and put together has not been put together correctly."While ex-Man Utd striker Wayne Rooney, added: "I know what it is like from managing Derby County when they had a points deduction. The mindset and message to the players was simple – just try to win the next game."All the noise around the club, from the media and other fans, will make them even hungrier to succeed."They could be fighting for the title or fighting for relegation by the end of the season. Who knows what's going to happen."As City walked off, they were accompanied by the taunt of "You're going down" from the Kop.City's fans answered with the trademark: "We're not really here."This, in essence, is what makes this Premier League campaign one that might yet be rendered void. City might win the title - but who knows if they will be here next season?As Maresca's side move into top gear and threaten to accelerate away from the chasing pack with wins such as this, no-one has a clue what their final destination will be.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Liverpool fans held up banners about Manchester City being found guilty of breaking financial rulesFigure caption, Highlights: Manchester City beat Liverpool to extend perfect start

schema.headline: Manchester City: A statement win but does it carry weight in a season of limbo?

title: Drumcree: It's within DUP's gift to remove O'Neill as first minister, says Lockhart
description: The DUP (Democratic Unionist Party) share power with Sinn Féin in the Northern Ireland Executive, but Lockhart says it can no longer be business as us
body: The DUP (Democratic Unionist Party) share power with Sinn Féin in the Northern Ireland Executive, but Lockhart says it can no longer be business as usual."You can not continue to engage with someone who is so blatant in her disregard and disdain for a large section of this community," she said. "Very clearly it cannot be business as usual at Stormont."Lockhart says her party must take action against O'Neill. "People want to see consequences, and we have said very clearly, profound consequence, and therefore we should use whatever is in our armoury to ensure that Michelle O'Neill, the person who really is supposed to be that first minister for all, as she claims, is dealt with in the appropriate way," she added.The DUP could remove O'Neill from the first minister's position if the deputy first minister quits. That role is held by Emma Little-Pengelly, but that seems unlikely.Sinn Féin assembly member John O'Dowd rejected claims that the move to ban the parade went in favour of his party, saying "the decision went in the way of the residents" who he said have "faced an awful four weeks" since the application to walk was lodged.O'Dowd, who is also finance minister in the executive, was one of a number of Sinn Féin politicians who joined a protest with residents on the Garvaghy Road.On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.Speaking on BBC News NI's Sunday Politics programme, O'Dowd said: "I own my decision", adding that he thinks it was "the right thing to do"."I got into politics to stand against the intimidation of communities such as the Garvaghy Road, who went through hell and high water over many, many years."I stood with the people of the Garvaghy Road. I will continue to stand with the people of Garvaghy Road because it was the right thing to do."He added that he believes the community responded in "a peaceful, democratic way" to the decision to approve a march on 27 September."I would appeal, not only to Gavin, but maybe hopelessly to Carla and others, to calm their language and to show responsible leadership and calm leadership at this stage," he added."I don't think that continued demonisation or an attempt to criminalise the community of the Garvaghy Road is an appropriate way forward."What we need in Portadown is reconciliation."

schema.headline: Drumcree: It's within DUP's gift to remove O'Neill as first minister, says Lockhart

title: PM says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit referendum
description: Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany. The
body: Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany. The prime minister told The Rest is Politics podcast, external that upon arriving in No 10, he had asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was.""I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas," he added.Burnham did not provide further details about the type or extent of Moscow's activity during the Brexit referendum.Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, said Burnham's comments were "another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016". It said that foreign interference in UK elections was "obviously unacceptable" but added: "There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum in 2016. "It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped."In his interview, due to be released on Monday, Burnham said he had discussed the problem of Russian interference with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his visit to Germany earlier this week."There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics," he said.He continued: "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."It is the first time a UK prime minister has said Russia sought to sway the 2016 Brexit poll but there have long been warnings about efforts by the Kremlin to exert influence on UK politics. In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee published a report into Russian interventions in UK elections and referendums.It did not provide a definitive conclusion on whether Russia had attempted to influence the results of the EU referendum but did criticise successive governments for failing to fully assess or counter the threat.In response, the Russian foreign minister dismissed the report out of hand and called it "Russophobia".And a Kremlin spokesman said Russia did not meddle in other countries' elections.In the same year, however, the then-Conservative government said it was "almost certain that Russian actors sought to interfere" in the 2019 general election.BBC Verify has tracked Russian-linked disinformation campaigns including using AI to create fake videos which impersonate journalists and news organisations reporting on Ukraine. One fake news website falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a discounted price.Earlier this year, Vijay Rangarajan, head of the UK Electoral Commission, told MPs that Russian deepfake videos had been "used extensively in elections around the world"."There is no reason to assume Britain would be an exception," he added. Last month, during his speech to the United Nations, Burnham accused Russian agencies of using "every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears".He announced that the UK would set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation. A Downing Street spokesperson said: "We are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values."We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies."

schema.headline: PM says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit referendum

title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
description: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.The attacks h
body: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children."These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services. Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker."We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday. "In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right."Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".Thousands of Polish ‌police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

schema.headline: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says

title: Sacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino's West End play
description: Borat actor Sacha Baron Cohen will star in a new play in London's West End from Hollywood director Quentin Tarantino.The Popinjay Cavalier, set in 183
body: Borat actor Sacha Baron Cohen will star in a new play in London's West End from Hollywood director Quentin Tarantino.The Popinjay Cavalier, set in 1830s Europe, was announced earlier this year and is the first play to be written for stage by the US filmmaker, who is also set to direct.Baron Cohen said he was "beyond delighted" to be working with Tarantino, saying: "When the best director in the world calls, you don't ask questions."The director, best known for violent film classics Pulp Fiction and Reservoir Dogs, has said he is "keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out".The play is set to premiere in March next year, with tickets available from Monday.The production was announced in March this year as a "rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise inspired by the grand swashbuckling epics of stage and screen".Baron Cohen, 54, is known for his self-created comic characters including infamous spoof wannabe gangster Ali G, Kazakh reporter Borat Sagdiyev, and Austrian fashionista Brüno Gehard.He has won two Baftas and three Golden Globes, as well as being nominated for three Oscars and six Emmys.The full cast for The Popinjay Cavalier is planned to be announced at a later date.The play will be co-produced by Sony Pictures Entertainment, which distributed Tarantino's most recent film Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood, and Sonia Friedman Productions, which has overseen hits like Harry Potter and the Cursed Child and Paddington the Musical.The director has repeatedly spoken about planning to retire from movies after making 10 films.He has made nine so far - he counts Kill Bill Volumes One and Two together - and has won two Oscars, for writing Pulp Fiction and Django Unchained.Tarantino revealed his plan to stage a play last summer, telling the Church of Tarantino podcast it was "all written"."It is absolutely the next thing I'm going to do. We'll start the ball rolling on it in January. It's probably going to take up a year and a half to two years of my life, if it's a success and I've got to do the tour version of it and all that," he said."I'm preparing for it to be a success. If it's a flop, I'll be done very quickly."The Popinjay Cavalier will premiere at the Phoenix Theatre on 18 March 2027, with tickets starting from £25.The 63-year-old director lives in Tel Aviv with his Israeli wife, Daniella Pick, and their two children. He told the podcast last year that he would "more than likely move to England and bring my family with me" while working on the play.Tarantino is also known for his forthright personality and made headlines at the end of last year for launching a stinging criticism of actor Paul Dano, as well as in March this year for a spat with Pulp Fiction actress Rosanna Arquette after she criticised the use of the N-word in the 1994 film.

schema.headline: Sacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino's West End play

title: AI is less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says
description: Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety r
body: Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released.His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals.But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology its a threat to humanity.The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown, but Trump has pushed against this.Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated."Let's get started today," he said. He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way. He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue.  He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology."We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute, external, launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute."In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best."Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI.Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins".However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU."In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said."When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived. "Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country."

schema.headline: AI is less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says

title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns
description: The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influe
body: The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said.It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up. The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation". However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home."But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together."He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring."A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said."Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course."Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world.These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps. The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey.Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said.Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30.However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues.But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn. That is less than the £24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR). Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale.However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain. And the official forecast from the OBR - which the chancellor relies on when making his plans - may come to a very different conclusion.The IFS reckons that to maintain departments' budgets in the face of higher inflation, the government may need to find an extra £25bn in 2029-30.That is before consider considering the ambition to raise defence spending. Raising such an amount would point to significant tax rises.The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different.But the IFS warned that the spending plans inherited from the previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, would mean some departments' budgets would not keep pace with inflation in a few years time.It said not addressing this would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans.However, previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line.

schema.headline: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns

title: Yandex: Ukraine strikes data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
description: Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said i
body: Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.

schema.headline: Yandex: Ukraine strikes data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
